## Why This Prototype Exists

I am preparing to teach MATH 346, and I do not think that teaching the course exactly as it was taught before is the right approach in the LLM era.

Students will use AI tools. The course should therefore teach them how to program, test, debug, interpret results, and critically inspect AI-generated code or explanations. The goal is not to make the course about AI. The goal is to teach mathematical and statistical software in a world where AI assistance is part of the working environment.

## How The Prototype Was Built

I used the existing course slides as a starting point for the syllabus topics and progression. With Codex, I then prepared this prototype website, rewriting the materials around problem-focused computational work, validation habits, and responsible AI use.

The site does not redistribute copyrighted slide decks, textbook PDFs, answer keys, exams, or private student work. It contains original course materials and starter code prepared for this redesign.

## What To Review First

Weeks 1-4 are the validated prototype. Weeks 5-15 have now been expanded
using the same teaching pattern:

| Week | Focus | Suggested review |
|---:|---|---|
| [Week 1](weeks/week-01.qmd) | MATLAB arrays, scripts, and plots | Look at the survival checklist, lab, and AI critique activity. |
| [Week 2](weeks/week-02.qmd) | Functions, conditions, and tests | Look at the testing emphasis and AI debugging activity. |
| [Week 3](weeks/week-03.qmd) | Curve fitting, interpolation, and residual checks | Look at the model validation and overfitting critique. |
| [Week 4](weeks/week-04.qmd) | Numerical methods and 3D plotting | Look at the numerical checks, surface plots, and AI answer review. |
| [Week 5](weeks/week-05.qmd) | Symbolic mathematics and verification | Look at domain assumptions, the tank-design problem, and the independent numerical check. |
| [Week 6](weeks/week-06.qmd) | MATLAB-to-R transition and reproducible reports | Look at the syntax bridge, supplied report scaffold, checked plots, and AI causal-claim review. |
| [Week 7](weeks/week-07.qmd) | Data transformation as question-answering | Look at one-verb invariants, missing-row accounting, grouped denominators, and the AI question-drift audit. |
| [Week 8](weeks/week-08.qmd) | Exploratory data analysis | Look at variation, covariation, overplotting, anomaly handling, the EDA log, and the AI interpretation audit. |
| [Week 9](weeks/week-09.qmd) | Import contracts and tidy data | Look at the supplied synthetic CSV, explicit schemas, observation keys, and the AI reshape audit. |
| [Week 10](weeks/week-10.qmd) | Relational and typed data | Look at string and factor contracts, time-zone-aware parsing, unmatched rows, relationship declarations, and the partial-key AI join audit. |
| [Week 11](weeks/week-11.qmd) | Readable pipelines and function contracts | Look at named checkpoints, normal and edge-case tests, and the AI refactor behavior-drift audit. |
| [Week 12](weeks/week-12.qmd) | Vectorized thinking and visible iteration | Look at typed iteration, preallocated loops, complete batch status logs, and the AI dropped-failure audit. |
| [Week 13](weeks/week-13.qmd) | Model claims and diagnostic evidence | Look at row accounting, contextual coefficients, baseline comparison, residual and influence flags, and the AI interpretation audit. |
| [Week 14](weeks/week-14.qmd) | Many models and aligned evidence | Look at the fixed monthly model contract, retained fit objects, coefficient intervals, grouped sensitivity checks, and the AI model-ranking audit. |
| [Week 15](weeks/week-15.qmd) | Communication and evidence reconciliation | Look at the generated evidence bundle, figure and caption contract, clean-run rehearsal, cross-artifact checks, and the AI conclusion audit. |

Weeks 1-4 have now been validated as the prototype pattern for the course.
Weeks 5-15 are developed and ready for review, but have not yet been
designated as validated prototypes. The full weekly arc is now available for a
course-wide coherence and workload review.

## What Feedback Would Help

I would especially appreciate feedback on these questions:

- Does the redesign still respect the spirit and content of the existing course?
- Are Weeks 1-4 realistic for two 75-minute meetings per week?
- Is the new Week 5 symbolic unit a realistic final MATLAB block, especially
  its fixed-volume tank example and verification workload?
- Does Week 6 give students with little programming experience enough support
  when moving from MATLAB to R and editing their first supplied `.qmd` report?
- Does Week 7 make the meaning of each `dplyr` transformation and its row-count
  consequences sufficiently explicit for beginners?
- Does Week 8 keep exploratory work disciplined enough by requiring findings,
  doubts, limitations, and next questions rather than polished conclusions?
- Does Week 9 make file paths, import schemas, row meaning, and observation-key
  checks manageable for beginners while still resembling real data work?
- Does Week 10 make strings, factors, date-times, key cardinality, unmatched
  rows, and composite joins manageable without overloading one week?
- Does Week 11 make readable pipeline structure, function contracts, and edge-
  case testing concrete enough for students who are still new to programming?
- Does Week 12 distinguish vectorization, typed iteration, and explicit loops
  clearly enough while making failed batch items impossible to overlook?
- Does Week 13 introduce regression interpretation and diagnostics without
  encouraging causal claims, automatic deletion, or trust in training fit?
- Does Week 14 make repeated modeling manageable without encouraging students
  to rank differently sized subsets by a single training metric or to hide
  sensitivity and uncertainty?
- Does Week 15 make the relationship among R source, CSV outputs, figures, PDF
  claims, clean-run reproducibility, and AI documentation manageable for a
  beginner group completing Project 2?
- Is the working assessment sequence realistic: quizzes in Weeks 3, 6, 9, and
  13, with the semester examination (midterm) in Week 8?
- Is the balance right between MATLAB/R skills, mathematical thinking, and validation?
- Do the LLM-related activities feel pedagogically useful rather than distracting?
- Are there essential commands, concepts, habits, or warnings missing from the full 15-week sequence?
- Does the approved [core/guided/extension workload model](weeks/workload-guide.qmd)
  make the 15-week resource bank realistic for beginners, and are any core
  selections still too ambitious?
- Does the [week-relative project sequence](projects/project-milestones.qmd)
  give beginners enough time to start without allowing Project 1 or Project 2
  to crowd out the transition weeks?

## The Intended Shift

The old version of the course naturally emphasized learning MATLAB and R command by command. That made sense before LLMs were widely available.

In this version, students still learn MATLAB and R, but each week is organized around a computational question:

1. What is the problem?
2. What representation or model should we use?
3. What code answers the question?
4. How do we know the result is correct?
5. What can an LLM help with, and what must we still verify ourselves?

The core skill I want students to leave with is not just the ability to run software. It is the ability to produce a computational result that they can defend.
